meta.title: Who really said "Give sorrow words; the grief that does not speak whispers the o'er-fraught heart and bids it break"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Shakespeare — but Malcolm says it, not Macbeth. Macbeth 4.3, first printed in the 1623 First Folio. The popular "knits up" wording is corrupt.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Give sorrow words; the grief that does not speak whispers the o'er-fraught heart and bids it break'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Shakespeare: Malcolm to Macduff in Macbeth, Act 4 Scene 3, first printed in the 1623 First Folio. The widely shared "knits up" version is a corruption.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: The line is Malcolm’s, spoken to Macduff in Macbeth, Act 4, scene 3, moments after Ross brings word that Macduff’s wife and children have been slaughtered. It was first printed in the 1623 First Folio, whose old-spelling text reads “Giue sorrow words; the griefe that do’s not speake, / Whispers the o’re-fraught heart, and bids it breake.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Whispers the o’re-fraught heart, and bids it breake”

source.excerpt:
ROSS: Your castle is surprised; your wife and babes / Savagely slaughter’d…

MALCOLM: Merciful heaven! / What, man! ne’er pull your hat upon your brows; / Give sorrow words: the grief that does not speak / Whispers the o’er-fraught heart and bids it break.

MACDUFF: My children too?
trail: The earliest text is the 1623 First Folio ↗, transcribed by Internet Shakespeare Editions, where Malcolm says: “Giue sorrow words; the griefe that do’s not speake, / Whispers the o’re-fraught heart, and bids it breake.”

There is no earlier printing to check against. The Folger’s editorial note states plainly that “Macbeth was first printed in the 1623 collection of Shakespeare’s plays now known as the First Folio” ↗, and that its own edition is based directly on that printing.
Modern editions keep the Folio’s wording. Folger ↗ prints “Whispers the o’erfraught heart and bids it break”; Shakespeare Navigators ↗ prints the same and glosses o’er-fraught as “over-burdened.”

Wikiquote’s Macbeth page independently lists the line at Act IV, Scene III ↗ in the same wording — and separately lists the Act II “knits up the ravell’d sleave of care” line that the corrupted variant appears to borrow from.
source.excerptNote: Modern-spelling text as printed by the MIT complete works ↗ and, with the same substantive wording, by the Folger Shakespeare Library ↗. The 1623 Folio spells it “Giue sorrow words; the griefe that do’s not speake, / Whispers the o’re-fraught heart, and bids it breake.”

source.rightsNote: The line comes from Macbeth, first published in the 1623 First Folio ↗ — more than three centuries before the 1931 US copyright cutoff, so the text is firmly in the public domain. No translation is involved: Shakespeare wrote in English, and the wording above is the Folio’s own, modernised only in spelling. Individual modern annotated editions may hold copyright in their notes and apparatus, but not in the words of the play.

author.name: William Shakespeare
author.heading: Shakespeare, and the man who actually says it
author.bio: Shakespeare wrote roughly three dozen plays for the London stage; Macbeth is among the shortest and bleakest of the tragedies, and was first performed in about 1606. Half his plays — Macbeth included — had never been printed when he died in 1616, and survive only because his colleagues gathered them into the 1623 First Folio. The speaker of this particular line is not Macbeth but Malcolm, the murdered king’s son, consoling Macduff.

misattribution.heading: The credit is right. The wording and the speaker often aren’t.
misattribution.intro: This is one of the rare famous-name quotations that survives scrutiny intact — Shakespeare really wrote it, and the wording above is the wording in the book. What goes wrong is downstream: a corrupted variant has overtaken the real one on quote sites, and the line is routinely put in the wrong character’s mouth.

items.why: The most-shared version online replaces whispers the o’er-fraught heart with knits up the o’er-wrought heart — a different verb and a different adjective. It is the form printed by Goodreads ↗, AZQuotes ↗ and QuoteFancy ↗, all crediting Macbeth. The earliest text does not support it: the 1623 Folio ↗ reads “Whispers the o’re-fraught heart.”

Offered as an observation rather than a documented finding: knits up is itself a genuine phrase from the same play — “Sleep, that knits up the ravell’d sleave of care,” which Wikiquote places at Act II, Scene II ↗. Two of the play’s best-known images about a mind under strain appear to have bled into one another.

The line is often quoted as if the title character said it. He does not. Folger’s text ↗ and the Shakespeare Navigators annotation ↗ both assign it to Malcolm, speaking to Macduff. Macbeth is the man who ordered the murders being grieved.

misattribution.truthLine: Shakespeare wrote it; Malcolm speaks it; and the authentic wording is whispers the o’er-fraught heart — exactly as the Folio-spelling text ↗ and modern scholarly editions print it.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: Malcolm does not say this in the abstract. Ross has just told Macduff that his castle was taken and his “wife and babes / Savagely slaughter’d,” and Macduff pulls his hat down over his face rather than let anyone see him. Malcolm’s answer — ne’er pull your hat upon your brows; give sorrow words — is an instruction to a man trying to hide, not a general maxim about feelings.

The image in the second line is precise and easy to lose. O’er-fraught means over-burdened, the way a ship is fraught with cargo; annotators gloss whispers here as “whispers to.” Grief that never gets spoken aloud does not go quiet — it goes inward, murmuring to an already overloaded heart until it gives way.
context.detailsSummary: Where the play is in this scene
detailsBody: The exchange sits at the end of Act 4, the long “England scene,” in which Malcolm has spent hundreds of lines testing whether Macduff can be trusted by falsely slandering himself. Ross’s news arrives just as that test ends, and the grief Malcolm invites Macduff to speak is what turns him into the man who will hunt Macbeth down.
Macbeth was never printed in Shakespeare’s lifetime. Every modern text of this speech descends from a single source: the copy set into type for the 1623 First Folio ↗, seven years after his death.
context.pull: Grief that stays unspoken does not go quiet. It goes inward.
